subcategory: native Willamette Valley wet prairie perennial

planting.note: Direct sow outdoors in fall so seed receives natural cold-moist stratification over winter; germination is slow and erratic, often extending into the following spring.

directions: Sow seed in fall into moist, fertile prairie or meadow soil in full sun, where plants will slowly form a basal clump of maple-shaped leaves before sending up tall, loosely branched spikes of rose-pink mallow flowers from late spring into midsummer. This tall checkerbloom is a signature forb of remnant Willamette Valley wet prairies and pairs naturally with camas and native bunchgrasses. Established plants tolerate seasonal winter wet and summer drought once their roots are deep, needing little supplemental water after the first year. Deadhead spent spikes to extend bloom and prevent excessive self-seeding in small gardens.

subcategory: native Pacific Northwest wet meadow perennial

planting.note: Sow directly after soil has warmed in spring, or set out fall-sown seedlings; unlike many prairie forbs this species germinates readily without extended cold stratification.

directions: Plant in consistently moist, fertile soil in full sun; this clump-forming iris relative produces grass-like blue-green foliage topped with violet-blue, yellow-throated flowers from late spring into early summer. It is one of the most common native wet-prairie and ditch-margin wildflowers of Willamette Valley and Puget Sound lowlands, readily self-sowing into small drifts. Each flower opens for a single day but clumps bloom over several weeks; cut back foliage after seed set to tidy the clump. Excellent at pond and rain-garden margins where soil stays damp through the growing season.

subcategory: native Pacific Northwest upland prairie perennial

planting.note: Direct sow in autumn into permanent, well-drained locations; the deep taproot resents transplanting, so avoid starting indoors or in containers.

directions: Sow into lean, well-drained upland prairie or rocky-bald soil in full sun; the dandelion-like yellow composite flowers open on slender stalks above a basal rosette of deeply cut leaves from April through June. Unlike wet-prairie companions such as camas and checkerbloom, silverpuffs favor the drier, better-drained swells within Willamette Valley and Puget lowland prairie mosaics. Mature seed heads form papery, silvery globes that give the species its common name and disperse readily by wind. Once established, the thick taproot makes this one of the more drought-tolerant native prairie forbs for a sunny, unirrigated bed.
sources: Humble Roots Farm Native Plant Nursery

subcategory: native Willamette Valley wet prairie perennial

planting.note: Sow fresh seed outdoors in fall; seed requires a prolonged cold-moist winter stratification and commonly does not germinate until the following spring.

directions: Plant in seasonally saturated prairie or swale soil in full sun, where fibrous-rooted clumps send up glossy, bright yellow five-petaled flowers from March into May, among the earliest bloomers in Willamette Valley wet prairies. Foliage and flowering depend on abundant spring moisture; the plant goes fully summer-dormant as prairie soils dry, so site it where it will not need irrigation once dormant. It spreads gradually by short rhizomes and self-sown seed to form loose colonies alongside camas and checkerbloom. Avoid rich, amended garden soil, which can make the plant leggy; it performs best in lean, naturally wet-in-winter clay.

subcategory: native Pacific Northwest prairie and oak-woodland-edge perennial

planting.note: Direct sow in fall or set out divisions; seed needs cold-moist stratification over winter and germination is typically sparse, slow, and spread over several months.

directions: Grow in dry-summer, well-drained soil at the dappled edge of oak woodlands or open prairie margins, where this low clump-forming violet bears golden-yellow flowers with fine maroon veining on the lower petal from April into June. It is an important larval host plant for fritillary butterflies, making it a valuable addition to Pacific Northwest pollinator and native plant gardens. Unlike many garden violets, it does not tolerate constantly moist soil and prefers to dry out in summer, reflecting its native habitat in oak savanna and prairie-edge plant communities of the Willamette Valley and Puget lowlands. Site at the transition between full prairie sun and the dappled shade of Garry oak or Douglas-fir canopy edges for best performance.
sources: Humble Roots Farm Native Plant Nursery

subcategory: native Pacific Northwest prairie and oak-savanna perennial (traditional food plant)

planting.note: Sow fresh seed directly in fall into well-drained, gravelly or rocky soil in its permanent spot; the deep taproot resents disturbance, and germination is slow, sometimes spanning more than one winter.

directions: Plant in lean, fast-draining prairie, bald, or oak-savanna soil in full sun, where blue-green, pinnately divided leaves with a strong celery-like aroma rise from a deep taproot each spring. Flat-topped clusters of small yellow flowers open in April and May, providing some of the earliest nectar for native bees and butterflies in Willamette Valley and Puget lowland prairies. Known traditionally among Pacific Northwest tribes as Indian celery, the aromatic leaves and seeds were used fresh, dried, or smoked as both food and medicine. Once its taproot is established, the plant is extremely drought tolerant and should never be irrigated in summer or grown in rich, moisture-retentive soil.
sources: Humble Roots Farm Native Plant Nursery

subcategory: native Pacific Northwest wet prairie bulb

planting.note: Plant corms 3-4 inches deep in fall in seasonally moist, humus-rich prairie or meadow soil; keep moist through winter and spring bloom, then let soil dry as the corm goes summer-dormant.

directions: Plant corms in fall among camas and other wet-prairie companions; grass-like leaves emerge in winter and dense umbels of white, faintly blue-veined star-shaped flowers open on wiry stems in May and June. Native to Willamette Valley and Puget lowland wet prairies, it shares the same vernally moist, summer-dry habitat preference as camas but blooms slightly later, extending the prairie floral display. Corms slowly multiply by offsets to form expanding colonies in undisturbed meadow plantings, and the bulbs were historically harvested and eaten by Indigenous peoples of the region. Allow foliage to yellow and die back naturally before mowing or cutting back, since the corm rebuilds its reserves during this period.
